subsection: H. Directors and Officers Liability (D&O) Insurance
text:
Chapter 3. Insurance and Indemnification
H. Directors and Officers Liability (D&O) Insurance
1. [3:645] Nature of Coverage: Directors and officers liability (D&O) insurance generally covers loss on account of claims
against directors and officers based upon defined “wrongful acts” committed in their corporate capacity, which may include
intentional misconduct (unlike CGL policies, which are based on an accidental “occurrence”; see ¶ 3:293).
2. [3:646] Typical Insuring Clause: “The Company shall pay on behalf of the Insured Persons [officers and directors] all Loss,
for which such Insured Person is not indemnified by the Insured Organization [corporation], and which such Insured Person
becomes legally obligated to pay on account of any claim[s] made against him, individually or otherwise … for a Wrongful Act
… [c]ommitted … or attempted by such Insured Person[s] before or during the Policy Period; and … [r]eported to the Company
… during the Policy Period …” [See Olson v. Federal Ins. Co. (1990) 219 CA3d 252, 258, 268 CR 90, 92 (emphasis added;
original emphasis omitted)]
3. [3:647] Coverage Analysis for Employment-Related Claims: The following are the primary issues in determining coverage
for claims under D&O policies:
a. [3:648] “Wrongful acts”: The term “wrongful act” is usually defined in the policy to include actual or alleged errors or
omissions, neglect or breach of duty, and misleading statements, including some forms of intentional conduct.
(1) [3:648.1] Does not include breach of contract: An insured's failure to pay amounts due under a contract does not
qualify as a “wrongful act.” Claims arising out of breach of contract thus are not covered because “there is no ‘wrongful
act’ and no ‘loss’ since the insured is simply being required to pay an amount it agreed to pay.” [August Entertainment,
Inc. v. Philadelphia Indemnity Ins. Co. (2007) 146 CA4th 565, 579, 52 CR3d 908, 918]
b. [3:649] Acts within official capacity: D&O policies typically limit coverage to “wrongful acts” by an officer or director
“in the discharge of his duties to the Insured organization in his Insured Capacity, or any matter claimed against him solely by
reason of his serving in such Insured Capacity.” [See Olson v. Federal Ins. Co., supra, 219 CA3d at 258-259, 268 CR at 92]
• [3:650] Therefore, there is no coverage for acts unrelated to the officer's or director's duties to the corporation. [Olson
v. Federal Ins. Co., supra, 219 CA3d at 261, 268 CR at 94—no coverage for claims against director who was also part
owner of corporation for acts undertaken as part owner]
c. [3:651] Limitation—no coverage where no individual liability: There can be no D&O coverage for acts for which the
directors and officers cannot be held liable individually. For example, only the corporate employer is liable for age and
sex discrimination under the ADEA and Title VII; corporate officers and directors have no personal liability. [See Miller v.
Maxwell's Int'l, Inc. (9th Cir. 1993) 991 F2d 583, 587 (applying Calif. law)]
d. [3:652] Certain liabilities not insurable: D&O policies typically indemnify for “loss” incurred by the directors or officers
individually or indemnified by the insured organization. “Loss” is generally defined to exclude certain liabilities incurred by
the directors and officers, including:
 
— punitive or exemplary damages;
 
— criminal or civil fines or penalties imposed by law; and
 
— treble damages and other amounts deemed uninsurable by law.
2
e. [3:653] Often no coverage for corporation: Historically, D&O policies covered only the directors and officers of a
corporation individually for their wrongful acts; i.e., there was no entity coverage. This continues to be true for many D&O
policies today, although some policies now include entity coverage (see ¶ 3:664).
• [3:654] Assuming no entity coverage, there is no coverage for claims against the corporation based upon action taken by
its shareholders in establishing corporate policy. [See Olympic Club v. Those Interested Underwriters at Lloyd's London
(9th Cir. 1993) 991 F2d 497, 500 (applying Calif. law)—no coverage for race and gender discrimination claims against
private club based on its own policies, rather than on wrongful acts of its directors and officers individually]
• [3:655] Unless a D&O policy provides otherwise, it does not cover a corporation's respondeat superior liability for
wrongful acts by its officers and employees in the course and scope of their employment. Nor is coverage established by the
fact that the board of directors ratified such acts. [See Olympic Club v. Those Interested Underwriters at Lloyd's London,
supra, 991 F2d at 502—policy covered corporation's imputed liability for wrongful acts of its officers and directors]
[3:656 - 3:663] Reserved.
(1) [3:664] Compare—entity coverage: Many D&O policies today provide “entity coverage” for certain claims made
against the corporation directly, including respondeat superior liability for wrongful acts by the corporation's officers and
directors. Entity coverage was developed to avoid disputes regarding allocation of defense and settlement costs where
claims against insured officers and directors are joined with claims against the uninsured corporation (see discussion at ¶
3:705 ff.). [See Continental Cas. Co. v. Anne Arundel Comm. College (4th Cir. 1989) 867 F2d 800, 801]
Cross-refer: Entity coverage is discussed further in Croskey, Heeseman, Ehrlich & Klee, Cal. Prac. Guide: Insurance
Litigation (TRG), Ch. 7F.
f. [3:665] Claims-made coverage: D&O policies are generally written on a “claims-made” basis—i.e., they cover claims
first made against the insured director or officer during the term of the policy. A claim is “made” when the insured officer
or director receives it or learns of it (see ¶ 3:294). Some policies also require the insured to report the claim to the insurer
within the policy period (so-called “claims made and reported” coverage).
A threshold issue in the employment context is whether the employee has taken action that constitutes a “claim.”
The filing and service of a civil action would qualify as a claim under virtually any claims-made policy. However, events
preceding filing suit must also be evaluated as potential claims. In the employment context, this may include such events as:
 
— a disgruntled employee's threat of litigation;
 
— the filing of an EEOC or FEHA “charge”;
 
— the institution of an EEOC accusation.
(1) [3:666] Where policy defines “claim”: If the policy contains a definition of “claim,” that definition controls.
(a) [3:667] Typical definition: Many D&O policies contain a definition of claim that includes:
 
“judicial or administrative proceedings or written demand against a director or officer for which such
director or officer may be subjected to a binding adjudication of liability.”
[3:668 - 3:669] Reserved.
(b) [3:670] Coercive vs. conciliatory “administrative proceedings”: Whether an administrative proceeding before
a state or federal agency constitutes a “claim” under such a policy depends on whether the administrative agency has
coercive power (i.e., the power to impose “binding adjudication of liability”) or merely powers of conciliation.
1) [3:671] EEOC proceedings: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has powers of conciliation
only. The EEOC only investigates and seeks voluntary compliance. Thus, the filing of a charge with the EEOC
does not constitute a “claim.” [See Bensalem Township v. Western World Ins. Co. (ED PA 1985) 609 F.Supp. 1343,
1347-1348 (applying Penn. law)—complaint filed with EEOC and EEOC's subsequent correspondence to Township
advising it of discrimination charge did not constitute a claim because neither requested money or other relief nor
advised that a lawsuit was to follow]
3
2) [3:672] FEHA proceedings: The California Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) has powers of
both conciliation and coercion. Upon conclusion of its investigation of a charge of discrimination under the California
Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA, Gov.C. § 12900 et seq.), the DFEH may seek conciliation; issue a “right
to sue” letter to the employee, which is a prerequisite to the filing of a civil action by the employee; or bring a civil
action in the name of the DFEH on behalf of the person claiming to be aggrieved (Gov.C. § 12965(a), (c) (amended
Stats. 2021, Ch. 278; eff. 1/1/22)).
Cross-refer: The administrative enforcement scheme is discussed in greater detail at ¶ 7:1031 ff., 7:1050 ff.
• [3:672.1] Neither the employee's filing of a discrimination charge, nor the subsequent DFEH investigation,
conciliation or issuance of a “right to sue” letter would appear to constitute a “claim” because they do not result
in a binding adjudication of liability or an award of damages.
• [3:672.2] In contrast, the filing of a civil action by the DFEH (a “judicial proceeding”) would satisfy the definition
of “claim” for purposes of determining insurance coverage. [See Gov.C. § 12965(a)]
[3:673 - 3:674] Reserved.
(2) [3:675] Absent policy definition: Where the policy does not define “claim,” the common law definition will control:
i.e., a “claim” is a demand for something as a right or as due, as opposed to a mere inquiry requesting an explanation, or
a mere expression of dissatisfaction. [Abifadel v. Cigna Ins. Co. (1992) 8 CA4th 145, 160, 9 CR2d 910, 920]
• [3:676] Letters by the Federal Home Loan Bank Board to Bank's officers and directors ordering them to comply with
various operating restrictions and to perform duties owed to Bank constituted a “claim.” [Mt. Hawley Ins. Co. v. Federal
Sav. & Loan Ins. Corp. (CD CA 1987) 695 F.Supp. 469, 479-480 (applying Calif. law)]
• [3:677] But letters from a state agency warning that Bank was guilty of specific statutory and regulatory violations
and threatening formal regulatory enforcement proceedings and a subsequent cease and desist order did not constitute
a “claim” against the directors. [California Union Ins. Co. v. American Diversified Sav. Bank (9th Cir. 1990) 914 F2d
1271, 1276-1277 (applying Calif. law)]
• [3:678] Similarly, the mere threat of legal action does not constitute a claim. [Winkler v. National Union Fire Ins. Co.
of Pittsburgh (9th Cir. 1991) 930 F2d 1364, 1366 (applying Calif. law)]
• [3:679] On the other hand, a letter demanding monetary compensation for alleged employment discrimination and
threatening suit was a “claim” even though the letter did not mention a specific dollar amount: “[T]he insistence on
compensation by way of settlement in lieu of litigation constituted a demand for ‘civil damages or other relief’ within
the ordinary meaning of those words.” [Westrec Marina Mgmt., Inc. v. Arrowood Indem. Co. (2008) 163 CA4th 1387,
1393, 78 CR3d 264, 269—delay in reporting claim excused insurer's duty to indemnify or defend suit]
[3:680 - 3:689] Reserved.
4. [3:690] Relevant Exclusions: A D&O policy may specifically exclude employment-related claims. In the absence of such
an exclusion, several exclusions typically found in D&O policies may be relevant to such claims:
a. [3:691] “Insured vs. insured” exclusion: D&O policies typically exclude coverage for actions brought by one insured
director or officer against another (usually excepting shareholder derivative suits). For example:
 
— “In consideration of the premium charged, it is hereby agreed that the Insurer shall not be liable to make any payment for
loss … under this policy in connection with any claim or claims made against the Insureds by an Insured as defined in
this policy, including the Company … except for stockholders' derivative actions brought by a shareholder of the Company
other than an Insured.” [See Conklin Co., Inc. v. National Union Fire Ins. Co. (D MN 1987) 1987 WL 108957, *1 (emphasis
added)]
[3:691.1 - 3:691.4] Reserved.
(1) [3:691.5] Purpose: One purpose of the insured vs. insured exclusion is to prevent collusive suits by corporations trying
to recoup corporate losses by attributing them to the wrongdoing of directors and officers who, if insured, have nothing to
4
lose by taking the blame. [See Biltmore Assocs., LLC v. Twin City Fire Ins. Co. (9th Cir. 2009) 572 F3d 663, 668 (applying
Ariz. law)]
But the exclusion is not limited to collusive suits. Rather, it precludes coverage for any internal dispute between the
corporation and its officers or directors, as well as for disputes between or among them personally. [American Med.
Int'l, Inc. v. National Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh (9th Cir. 2001) 244 F3d 715, 723 (applying Calif. law); Level 3
Communications, Inc. v. Federal Ins. Co. (7th Cir. 1999) 168 F3d 956, 958 (applying Neb. law)]
(2) [3:692] Wrongful termination claims by former officer? It is unclear whether the insured vs. insured exclusion bars
coverage for wrongful termination and breach of contract claims by former corporate officers against the corporation. The
dispositive issue appears to be whether the former officer is suing in the former officer's capacity as an “insured” (i.e., officer
or director). [See Foster v. Kentucky Housing Corp. (ED KY 1994) 850 F.Supp. 558, 561 (applying Ky. law)—exclusion
applicable; compare Conklin Co., Inc. v. National Union Fire Ins. Co. (D MN 1987) 1987 WL 108957 (applying Minn.
law)—exclusion not applicable where plaintiff suing in capacity as former employee rather than as discharged officer]
(a) [3:692.1] Policy provisions: To address this issue, some policies now specifically provide that “this exclusion shall
not apply to a wrongful termination of employment claim brought by a former employee other than a former employee
who is or was a Director of the Company.” [See Bernstein v. Genesis Ins. Co. (ND IL 2000) 90 F.Supp.2d 932, 936
(emphasis added) (applying Ill. law); Biltmore Assocs., LLC v. Twin City Fire Ins. Co., supra, 572 F3d at 668—“insured
vs. insured exclusion” excepted claims by former officers and directors for wrongful termination, discrimination or
sexual harassment]
[3:693] Reserved.
b. [3:694] “Bodily injury” exclusion: D&O policies typically contain an exclusion for bodily injury. (E.g., “This policy does
not cover … loss arising out of claims for bodily injury, sickness, disease, death or emotional distress.”)
Employment-related claims alleging physical or emotional injury would appear to be subject to this exclusion.
(1) [3:695] Emotional distress also excluded: Claims for emotional distress are not covered under liability insurance
where the underlying acts are not covered: “Any damages flowing from noncovered losses that may lead to emotional
distress cannot be used to expand coverage where none was intended or bargained for by the parties.” [Waller v. Truck Ins.
Exch., Inc. (1995) 11 C4th 1, 16, 44 CR2d 370, 376]
c. [3:696] “Intentional injury” exclusion: D&O policies typically do not include an express “intentional injury” exclusion.
Nonetheless, Ins.C. § 533 bars indemnification for “loss resulting from the wilful act of the insured” (see ¶ 3:105 ff.).
This has been interpreted to bar coverage under CGL policies for claims of sexual harassment (see ¶ 3:447) and tortious
termination of employment in violation of public policy (Tameny claims) (see ¶ 3:426). The same result would likely apply
to coverage under D&O policies.
[3:697 - 3:704] Reserved.
5. Allocation of Defense and Settlement Costs
a. [3:705] Joinder of claims: Where claims covered under a D&O policy (e.g., claims against the officers or directors) are
joined in litigation with other, uncovered claims (such as claims against the corporation itself), the insurer's obligations to
reimburse settlement and defense costs must be allocated or apportioned among the claims and parties involved. [Raychem
Corp. v. Federal Ins. Co. (ND CA 1994) 853 F.Supp. 1170, 1180 (applying Calif. law); Safeway Stores, Inc. v. National Union
Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, Penn. (9th Cir. 1995) 64 F3d 1282, 1287 (applying Calif. law)]
(1) [3:706] Compare—no allocation for respondeat superior liability: The insurer is not entitled to an allocation of
settlement and defense costs where the insured corporation is sued solely on the basis of vicarious liability for wrongful
acts by its officers/directors. Assuming coverage, the corporation is entitled to full reimbursement of all settlement costs
where its liability is purely derivative. [Nordstrom, Inc. v. Chubb & Son, Inc. (9th Cir. 1995) 54 F3d 1424, 1432 (applying
Wash. law); Safeway Stores, Inc. v. National Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, Penn., supra, 64 F3d at 1287]
b. [3:707] Joinder of claims against noninsured parties: Allocation may also be required where claims against insured
5
officers and directors are joined with claims against other (noninsured) agents and employees of the corporation. [Harbor Ins.
Co. v. Continental Bank Corp. (7th Cir. 1990) 922 F2d 357, 368 (applying Ill. law)—Bank paid $17.5 million in settlement
of suit against certain directors (insureds) and other agents and employees (noninsured): D&O insurer obligated to reimburse
Bank only for that portion of settlement attributable to the directors' wrongful acts]
c. [3:708] Joinder of uninsured claims: Where the corporation chooses to indemnify its officers and directors for noncovered
liabilities, an allocation of liability must be made between the D&O insurer and the corporation.
(1) [3:709] Allocation of defense costs: Most courts hold that where a suit alleges both covered and noncovered claims
against insured officers and directors, the D&O insurer is obligated to pay only those defense costs “generated in defense
of covered claims.” [Okada v. MGIC Indem. Corp. (9th Cir. 1986) 823 F2d 276, 282 (applying Hawaii law)]
However, if the defense expenditure is “reasonably related” to the defense of a covered claim, it can be allocated solely
to the covered claim, even if it also aids in the defense of noncovered claims. [Safeway Stores, Inc. v. National Union
Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, Penn., supra, 64 F3d at 1289 (applying Calif. law)—defense costs “reasonably related” to
defense of insured directors and officers must be paid by D&O insurer even if payment benefits uninsured party (the
corporation)]
(2) [3:710] Allocation of settlement costs: When a settlement resolves both covered and noncovered claims, the insurer
may attempt to allocate the settlement amounts.
(a) [3:711] Allocation denied unless “larger settlement” due to uninsured claim: Several courts have allowed a
corporation to obtain reimbursement of all settlement costs where its liability is purely derivative of the liability of its
insured directors and officers. Allocation is appropriate only to the extent settlement and defense costs were increased
due to corporate liability that is not “concurrent” with the liability of its directors and officers. [Safeway Stores, Inc.
v. National Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, Penn., supra, 64 F3d at 1287; Nordstrom, Inc. v. Chubb & Son, Inc. (9th
Cir. 1995) 54 F3d 1424, 1432 (applying Wash. law)]
(b) [3:712] Other cases allocate settlement costs based on “relative exposure”: Some other decisions allow allocation
of settlements according to each defendant's “relative exposure,” making it less likely that the D&O insurer will be
responsible for the entire settlement. [Slottow v. American Cas. Co. of Reading, Penn. (9th Cir. 1993) 10 F3d 1355,
1359 (applying Calif. law)]
Comment: Subsequent Ninth Circuit decisions have interpreted Slottow's “relative exposure” analysis to apply only
where the parties have already agreed to an allocation; i.e., Slottow did not address an insurer's right to allocate in the
absence of such agreement. [See Nordstrom, Inc. v. Chubb & Son, Inc., supra, 54 F3d at 1435]
(3) [3:713] Burden of proof: Several cases hold that while the insured must first demonstrate that a loss falls within the
coverage of the policy, the burden then shifts to the insurer to demonstrate that the settlement amount was increased due
to the liability of the corporation or an uninsured third party. [See Safeway Stores, Inc. v. National Union Fire Ins. Co. of
Pittsburgh, Penn., supra, 64 F3d at 1288-1289; and Nordstrom, Inc. v. Chubb & Son, Inc., supra, 54 F3d at 1434]
➪ [3:714] PRACTICE POINTER: While insurers will often contend that all or most of the settlement or defense costs in
a case should be allocated to the uninsured corporation, counsel for insureds (whether representing individual directors or
officers or the corporation) may be able to resist such allocation based on the fact that covered claims against the directors
and officers are intertwined with and inseparable from noncovered claims.
Cross-refer: Directors and Officers liability insurance is discussed in greater detail in Croskey, Heeseman, Ehrlich &
Klee, Cal. Prac. Guide: Insurance Litigation (TRG), Ch. 7F.
[3:715 - 3:724] Reserved.
